```{r library}
library(diplomacyR)
```

Diplomacy is a negotiation game, and no program plays it well. The bots in
this package are not an attempt to change that. They exist so that a position
can be played forward without a table of seven people, so that a rules change
or a map variant can be exercised over thousands of turns, and so that
questions about the board itself — which provinces get fought over, how long
games run, whether the map is balanced — can be answered with data rather
than assertion.

## Legal orders come first

Every bot picks its orders out of `dp_legal_orders()`, which enumerates
exactly the orders the rules permit in the current phase. A bot therefore
cannot emit an illegal order, whatever else it gets wrong.

```{r legal}
game <- dp_new_game()
legal <- dp_legal_orders(game, "Italy")
table(legal$type)
```

```{r legal-head}
head(legal, 4)
```

The enumeration is exhaustive, convoyed moves included, so it is also the
right thing to hand to a user interface that wants to offer a menu — which is
precisely what the bundled **shiny** order editor does.

## The four bots

`dp_ai_orders()` produces a complete order set for one power.

**`"hold"`** is the passive baseline. Every unit holds; forced to act, it
retreats to the first open province, builds armies at home, and lets the
civil-disorder rule choose its disbands.

```{r hold}
dp_ai_orders(game, "Italy", bot = "hold")
```

**`"random"`** picks uniformly among each unit's legal orders. It is the
baseline any other strategy has to beat, and it is the useful one for
stress-testing the engine, because it generates positions no human would ever
write.

```{r random}
set.seed(42)
dp_ai_orders(game, "Turkey", bot = "random")
```

**`"greedy"`** walks each unit towards the nearest supply centre it does not
already own, refuses to send two of its own units to the same province, and
then converts the units with nothing better to do into support for its own
attacks. It plays a recognisable, if crude, opening.

```{r greedy}
dp_ai_orders(game, "France", bot = "greedy")
```

**`"negotiator"`** is greedy play plus a crude substitute for diplomacy: it
treats the board leader as the common enemy and leaves the weakest power
alone. There is no negotiation protocol in the package, so this is a stand-in
for the part of the game a program cannot play. It is marked experimental for
that reason.

```{r negotiator}
dp_ai_orders(game, "Russia", bot = "negotiator")
```

`dp_ai_all()` does all seven powers at once, and takes either one bot name
for everybody or a named vector mapping powers to bots.

```{r ai-all}
set.seed(3)
orders <- dp_ai_all(game, bots = c(France = "greedy", England = "random"))
orders[orders$power %in% c("England", "France"), ]
```

Powers not named in the vector fall back to the greedy bot.

## Playing a game out

`dp_step()` resolves one phase; any power you do not supply orders for is
played by `bots`.

```{r step}
dp_step(game, bots = "greedy")
```

`dp_play()` repeats that until someone controls 18 centres, until only one
power is left, or until the turn cap. It returns a `dp_history` recording
every turn.

```{r play}
history <- dp_play(bots = "greedy", max_years = 3, seed = 2024)
history
```

Three years is a very short game — the cap is there to keep this vignette
quick — so the outcome is a draw. The history is the interesting part.

```{r history}
head(as_tibble(history), 4)
```

`dp_power_summary()` reduces a history to one row per power, with the peak
each power reached as well as where it finished.

```{r summary}
dp_power_summary(history)
```

`dp_sc_trajectory()` gives the same data restricted to movement phases, which
is the natural series to plot, and `dp_plot_sc_history()` plots it. The
dashed line is the 18 centres a solo victory needs.

```{r trajectory}
dp_plot_sc_history(history)
```

## Batch simulation

`dp_simulate()` plays many games and collects the outcomes. It is the slow
function in the package — a full-length game is several hundred
adjudications — so keep `n` and `max_years` modest while you are exploring,
and pass `verbose = FALSE` when you do not want a line per game.

```{r simulate}
sim <- dp_simulate(
  n = 3, bots = "greedy", max_years = 3, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE
)
sim
```

The `dp_sim` object holds a per-game outcome table, final centre and unit
counts for every power in every game, and a tally of contested provinces.

```{r sim-games}
sim$games
```

`dp_stats()` summarises it three ways. `"power"` is one row per power:

```{r stats-power}
dp_stats(sim, "power")
```

`"outcome"` is the split between solo victories and draws, and `"length"` the
distribution of game lengths:

```{r stats-outcome}
dp_stats(sim, "outcome")
dp_stats(sim, "length")
```

Every game here ran into the turn cap, so both tables have a single row. Over
a real run at the default cap of twenty years they are the two summaries you
actually want.

`summary()` on a simulation is `dp_stats(sim, "power")`, and
`dp_power_summary()` works on games, histories and simulations alike.

## Analysis plots

Three plot functions take a `dp_sim` directly. All of them return **ggplot2**
objects, so they can be themed, faceted or combined like any other plot.

`dp_plot_winrates()` charts solo victories by power. Over a short run like
this one there are none to chart — a solo needs far more than three years —
but over a long run this is the balance question in one picture.

```{r winrates}
dp_plot_winrates(sim)
```

`dp_plot_centres()` shows the distribution of final supply-centre counts,
which says more than the win rate does when most games end in a draw.

```{r centres}
dp_plot_centres(sim)
```

`dp_plot_supply_heatmap()` puts the standoff tally back on the board, shading
each province by how often a move bounced there. With three short games there
is almost nothing to see; the point of the chart is the pattern that emerges
over hundreds.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 6.8}
dp_plot_supply_heatmap(sim)
```

## Building your own bot

There is no plug-in mechanism, and there does not need to be one. A bot is
any function that takes a game and a power and returns a `dp_orders` tibble;
`dp_legal_orders()` gives you the candidate set, and `dp_bind_orders()`
assembles the answer. Here is one that holds on supply centres it already
owns and otherwise moves at random:

```{r custom-bot}
dig_in <- function(game, power) {
  legal <- dp_legal_orders(game, power)
  mine <- names(game$sc_owner)[game$sc_owner == power]
  on_sc <- legal$loc %in% mine & legal$type == "hold"
  score <- ifelse(on_sc, 2, runif(nrow(legal)))
  keep <- vapply(split(seq_len(nrow(legal)), legal$loc),
                 function(i) i[which.max(score[i])], integer(1))
  legal[sort(keep), ]
}
```

On the opening position it would simply hold everything, because every unit
starts on a centre its own power owns. A mid-game position gives it something
to do:

```{r custom-bot-run}
mid <- dp_example_game("midgame")
set.seed(1)
dig_in(mid, "Russia")
```

Warsaw, Sevastopol and Sweden are Russian centres and sit tight; the army in
Ukraine, which is on no centre at all, is left to the coin toss.

Feed the result to `dp_adjudicate()` or `dp_step()` exactly like any other
order set.

```{r custom-bot-step}
set.seed(1)
dp_step(mid, orders = dig_in(mid, "Russia"), bots = "greedy")
```
